stem: A developer's request includes three tool definitions but sets `tool_choice` to force one specific named tool. Are the other two tools' definitions still sent as part of the request, even though they can't be called this time?
explanation: Yes; all defined tools in the tools array are still sent as part of the request (and count toward token usage) regardless of the `tool_choice` setting, since `tool_choice` only controls which tool(s) the model is permitted/required to actually call, not which tool definitions are included in the request payload itself, meaning removing genuinely irrelevant tools from the array (not just relying on `tool_choice`) is the way to actually reduce their token cost.
reference: All defined tools are sent regardless of tool_choice restriction

choices.text: Yes; all defined tools are still sent and count toward token usage regardless of `tool_choice`, since `tool_choice` only controls which tool(s) can be called, not which definitions are included; removing tools from the array is what reduces their cost.
choices.reasoning: Correct: `tool_choice` and the tools array are separate concerns, `tool_choice` restricts what can be called, but doesn't remove other tool definitions from the request payload or their associated token cost; actually omitting irrelevant tools from the array is the real cost-reduction lever.

choices.text: No; setting `tool_choice` to force a specific tool automatically removes the other tool definitions from the request and their token cost.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: `tool_choice` doesn't affect which tool definitions are included in the request; all tools in the tools array are still sent and billed regardless of the `tool_choice` restriction.

choices.text: This consideration only applies if using the Batches API.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this relationship between `tool_choice` and the tools array applies to real-time requests just as well as batch requests.

choices.text: This consideration only applies to built-in, server-side tools.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this consideration about tool definitions still being sent regardless of `tool_choice` applies to custom, client-defined tools just as much as any other category.

stem: Does a developer need to implement the MCP protocol's low-level message-passing details themselves from scratch, or are there existing SDKs/libraries that handle this?
explanation: There are existing SDKs/libraries (similar in spirit to the official Claude API SDKs) that implement the MCP protocol's low-level details, letting a developer build an MCP client or server using higher-level APIs rather than implementing the raw protocol message format and handling from scratch, which significantly reduces the implementation effort needed to adopt MCP.
reference: Existing SDKs handle MCP's low-level protocol details

choices.text: There are existing SDKs/libraries implementing MCP's low-level details, letting a developer build a client or server using higher-level APIs rather than implementing the raw protocol from scratch.
choices.reasoning: Correct: similar to how official Claude API SDKs wrap the raw HTTP API, MCP SDKs/libraries exist to handle the protocol's low-level message-passing details, significantly reducing the effort needed to build a compliant client or server.

choices.text: A developer must always implement the entire MCP protocol's raw message format from scratch, with no existing libraries available.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this overstates the implementation burden; existing SDKs/libraries are available specifically to reduce this effort, similar to how the Claude API has official SDKs.

choices.text: MCP has no defined protocol format at all; each implementation invents its own ad hoc approach.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: MCP is specifically a defined, standardized protocol, not something left to ad hoc, incompatible implementations; that standardization is exactly its core value proposition.

choices.text: This question is irrelevant since MCP cannot actually be implemented by third-party developers.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: MCP is specifically designed to be implementable by any developer/organization, which is central to its interoperability goal.
